title: Your People Are The Future Of Your Brand

segments.text: I would love for you to now get all the stamina together and give him a warm welcome. Ash, would you join us? Thank you.
>> Thank you. Good morning. Good morning. Uh So, my talk is around this idea how your people are the future of your brand and
the internet is well, it's always been a very busy place and I think we all know that it's about to get 10 times busier.
Uh and the reason for that is the rise of AI-generated content has now overtaken the amount of human content on the internet. So, we have that issue.
And then the other issue that we have is that people don't trust brands anymore. 71% say they trust brands less today than they did a year ago. Trust in
brands and corporations is on the decline. So, with those two things in mind, brands now have a problem. How do you recruit the best talent? How
do you influence a market? How do you stand out amongst the noise? How do you promote your employer brand, as we just heard on there?
The answer is sitting in offices around the world right now. In that the answer is in people. And there's a bit of what I call a
people flywheel that exists at the center of every brand and company, where we all know the saying people buy from people, but it's much broader than this.
In that people also join companies for people, they stay in companies for people, >> [snorts] >> they follow people, they trust people. We know the impact that people have in
companies and there's almost like a a center of this. And the problem is a a of the time that those people within companies to the
wider world are mostly invisible. And I've been in the business of essentially trying to make people visible for a decade now. And this was my second job on my LinkedIn in
the experience section. It says this little thing which says helping tell the fascinating story of one of the UK's fastest growing companies through the eyes of its CEO.
And my first job, I was a cleaner in a gym. Um and I loved that job and I missed that job. >> [laughter] >> Uh
and when I was a cleaner in that gym, I went to a rap event with a friend. And during the smoking break of this rap
event, I met a kid outside who was 18 years old at the time. And my friend said to me, I wanted to go to university to study marketing and try
to get a job that wasn't in a gym. And my friend said, "Oh, you should speak to that guy. He's starting a business. He's
just dropped out of university." So, I spoke to this guy and then afterwards, I sent him a message on Facebook. And this is the message that I sent and
the guy's name was Steven Bartlett. And you'll see the date, 2nd of May, 2012. Um and funnily enough, this is the first time I'd ever tried to network with
anyone which is probably like the greatest stroke of luck that I'll have in my life. Uh you see, I literally say, "I always get told networking is important." That
was my mom. My mom told me networking it was important. Um and I'm just starting out and I'm keen to learn. So, I messaged him
and I met up with him and we started working together on some stuff. And during those years from 2012 to 2014-15, I would always say to him that he should
start a YouTube channel. And he was talking about it on the podcast that he now has on YouTube. Um and at the time, he would dismiss the
idea, but eventually won him round and we started filming videos and making them and putting them out on the internet. And then fast forward
a couple years and that becomes my full-time job, my second job. I became a personal brand manager. Uh and this is me, Ash Jones, personal
brand manager for Steven Bartlett. And then fast forward to today and Steve has the second biggest podcast in the world. He's the youngest ever
dragon on the UK's BBC Dragons' Den. He's got over 10 million followers on social media and he's got a book that's sold well over a million copies now. And
off the back of working with Steve, I set up an agency called Great Influence. And at the time, it was the first ever personal branding
agency that specialized in founders and entrepreneurs. And I started that in 2018. And over the last seven, eight years or so, we've probably done around 2 billion views on content
for founders and entrepreneurs that we've worked with and grown them over 15 million followers. And also made another dragon um and a couple of best-selling authors
along the way. And the job that we were doing, essentially, was helping make people invisible. And we always had conversations with people, founders, entrepreneurs. We
never really had a brand come to us. It was always the founder of a brand come to us. And then in 2023, a company called Booking.com came to us.
Um and I was like, I wonder what they want because it's probably not the CEO. The CEO probably already has a comms team. Um and they actually proposed the idea
of this project to us that we've not done before and they said, "We've got a number of senior leaders within the company and we really want to try to get
them to be part of the amplification and promotion of our employer brand. And also, we have a number of strategic objectives within the company right now.
We're just moving into a new huge HQ in Amsterdam and we want to get people excited about that. We really want to showcase the culture and the leadership
styles of the people at Booking.com. So, they said, "Do you want to build a program together? And we'll build a leadership advocacy program." And so, we did that with Booking, which
was the first time we'd ever worked not with a founder or entrepreneur, just like a collective of people within a company. Um and we worked with 10 people in
total, which was across the C-suite, VPs, directors, and head ofs. Um and the result of doing that, we hit around 4 million impressions on
LinkedIn. Every leader that was in the cohort increased their on LinkedIn tenfold and all 10 of them joined the top 15 voices on LinkedIn within
Booking.com, which is around 20,000 people in the company. And so, about 3 or 4 months ago, after doing this with Booking for a couple of years and one or two other
businesses, I thought there's something in this. Um Um, and I was actually in Amsterdam last year, which is how I ended up here. I was speaking in Amsterdam.
Uh, and after that talk, I had the feeling that something was in the air um, with the conversations that I had with a lot of people in brands
afterwards on how much this was kind of starting to become on the radar for people. And I thought there's something in this. So, I set up a second agency
that is called In Good Company, and we essentially take that booking project of helping a brand activate their senior leadership teams on social. And
the reason why both of those companies exist really, whether it's the founder or the CEO or a wider group of people within the leadership team is that
brands have always been built on people. We know companies like Apple because of Steve Jobs and Virgin because of Richard Branson. And there's something that's changed now in
how brands have been built on people. The old way was you'd get them speaking at events, leaders speaking at events, or a CEO would have a quote in a press release,
or they'd do branded content. You see that in the past couple of years where a company will like sit down their director of HR and ask questions and put
the content out. Um, and that to me is the old way of doing things with people within a brand. And the new way is that the people
themselves are now the channel. And in the last couple of months there's a really good example of this. So, this is a woman called Katherine
Turner, and she works at Marks & Spencer's, which is a very big retailer in the UK. Um, and she started posting on TikTok. And she started going viral. And if you
look her up on TikTok, she's now become somewhat of a cult where people are making videos about her every single day near enough. Uh
and she's the director of product development for Marks & Spencer's food. And what she did was she started taking people behind the scenes of how Marks &
Spencer's decides and develops the food ranges that they do. And all of a sudden these videos started taking off. They start averaging 500,000 views a video.
And this is kind of the reason that I was speaking at that that event in Amsterdam that led to starting that business that I saw within booking of like when a
brand is brave enough to platform its leaders, incredible things can happen as people are now the channel. Um and almost overnight, I think the knock-on
effect of Katherine from Marks & Spencer's is quite significant in that what it may look like on the outset is just somebody making TikToks
and people commenting on them and getting lot lots of likes. Whereas actually, she's now one of their most like valuable recruiting tools. People will want to work at Marks & Spencer's
because they've seen Katherine Turner. Um she's also one of their most valuable consumer insights tool for Marks & Spencer's food. If you go on every
single one of the TikToks in the comments, all the team has to do is look in there to know which product they need to develop next because it's full of
people requesting Katherine to make these these products. Um so this was like a really timely thing that happened for the business that I was launching because
until that point, I was waiting for somebody like Katherine to show up and kind of grab the internet. Um and the timing of it was just really apt.
And is this working? Unfortunately, I kind of spent the last 2-3 months uh looking at the data of a lot of large organizations across the UK and Europe
and looking at their leadership teams to see what they were doing and to see if there was more Katherine Turners out there. Um And the data was really interesting in
that the average leadership team I say 70% of the senior leadership team across those levels I mentioned are invisible on LinkedIn. They don't post anything.
And then there's maybe the 30% that are visible only a small amount of them are actually posting content that is actually building any kind of authority within a
market. A lot of the time they are sharing a job post or doing a repost of something that's happened within the company or they're saying that they went
to an event or something like this. Um so the data shows us that we're still early on this. Like a lot of leadership teams are still invisible apart from
Marks & Spencer's. 97% of their leadership team are active on LinkedIn the last 90 days, which to me says a really interesting thing because Katherine was actually the
second person from Marks & Spencer's that I recognized. The first was their CEO Stuart, who has been doing something for the past 2 years essentially. He's
somebody that I've kind of used in numerous case studies and speaking um presentations as an example of a CEO at a large corporation doing something that
was forward-thinking. And him doing that no doubt influenced Katherine that's influenced the wider senior leadership team. So you can really see that this is
kind of something that has to be baked into the culture of a company for it to work. Um And with that level of invisibility like
average 70% of leadership teams being silent, there's also a cost to that for a company. We kind of worked out we're launching this as research next week Um
um and we've calculated the average cost for a large organization in the UK, which has like 2,000 employees, the cost per year annually would be
around 17.8 million pounds, which is about 20 million euros. Um and a lot of that is within recruitment and talent. So, like the cost of not having a strong
employer brand goes up as a result and those leaders can amplify that employer brand. Um and the cost to even replace those senior leaders, senior leaders are
more engaged with the company, the more that they actually talk about being part of that company. So, there's all these like knock-on effects that exist not
only across culture and talent and people, but across sales, across marketing, across PR and comms, across internal engagement, external engagement. I genuinely believe that a
group of leaders are one of the most interesting channels that exist within a business right now because of the breadth of impact that they have on the
success of a company if they're either positive or negative. And we know this because we've all been part of companies in times where either the company itself
is has a negative perception because of the group of people or there's one or two people within the company that give us a negative perception of it. Um and
people can really swing our perception of companies and brands whether we're internal working within them or externally within the market that they are trying to reach.
Um and Booking, for example, they had great people. Every company has great people. Like you go in any company and the senior leadership teams are filled with
great people. That's why people want to work in those places and they stay in those places. Um the problem was and one that I've seen that exists over the past
two, three months since launching this business and talking to these companies is that there's no system to build these channels essentially. Um and there's three problems really
that I think exist. One is that there's no ownership of it. So, I'll talk to one brand and they'll be like, "Oh, it's someone in comms that you would speak
to." I'll speak to another and it's like, "Oh, our employer brand does this." And then another would be PR and media, another sales, another talent.
Um there's no no connecting thread with any company that I speak to. So, I think the first issue is that there's no ownership internally really. It's just kind of
either left to It's almost like an add-on to someone's job most of the time, which for one of the most important set of channels
within business is a wild kind of thing to think. Or it's actually left to the leader themselves on top of their full-time job. Um
and then two is that there's an emotional element element for a lot of these leaders. It's the fear of like, "What if nobody cares about what I've
got to say? Or what if nobody actually engages with what I say?" And there's a bit of a seniority paradox that exists where the higher up in your career you
go, if you've not been used to putting yourself out there to start when you're 10, 15, 20 years into your career is an incredibly daunting thing because it's I
saw an image the other day that said the output of a per- perfectionist and it was just a blank page. And I think that's exactly what happens when senior
leaders try to show up visibly for the first time whether online or offline. If they do something like this, they go and speak for the first time and they've
been doing their career for 10, 15 years, they think that they should be perfect and they don't recognize that they're actually a beginner in just this
kind of setting. So, there's like an emotional element that exists [clears throat] with doing this as well. Um and then third is the tactics. They
don't actually know what to talk about. Uh, it's very daunting to sit at a blank page and go have an idea and say something. And your brain is just like
grasping at nothingness. Um, so that idea of like, what do I actually say, coupled with that idea of kind of trying to say the perfect thing means
that it's no surprise when I look at the data and probably 70% of leaders in companies are saying next to nothing. And all of these to me are just solvable
problems. Um, if you create the right system within a company and for the first one, you essentially implement an owner. So, someone whose job is making our
leadership visible. And when I started my second job, um, I think I was the maybe the first ever person with the title personal brand
manager as a full-time salary job. This was in 2015. Um, and now it's actually a viable career. Like, not only are companies hiring for it, you can start businesses
in it. You can become a freelancer consultant in it. There's multiple people that have left Great Influence and gone on to be consultants or
freelancers within the personal branding space. And I think the exact same thing is going to happen with this where in three, four, five years, one is going to
be common for this to be somebody's full-time job internally. It probably is within some companies, but it's going to be widespread. And then the second thing
that I think is going to happen is that it's going to become kind of part of the leadership role in some way, shape, or form. And companies
are going to have to figure out that piece as well. I know some companies actually KPI on it. Um, and I think there's an issue as well of like, how do
you reward for it as well? I actually made a Tik Tok about the Katherine Turner thing and I clicked on the insights and in the search after people
had watched my video, the top thing was does Katherine Turner get paid? So that in itself is like a thing that companies are going to start kind of
grappling with like how do you work with these leaders when they're building their own channels? But first implement an owner for it. And then number two,
there's a big coaching element here. A lot of the job that I've done over the past 10 years with founders and entrepreneurs and now into this, a lot
of it is just coaching people. A lot of it is like therapy and just giving them the confidence that their ideas are worth putting out into
the world is a huge chunk of it. So coaching leaders, how do they show up online? Who should they try to be? Who are the audiences that they're trying to
speak to? What What can they say? How can they say it? How can you give them the confidence to share it? And then three to help them know what to
talk about. And the ways that I've kind of done this over the past decade, I think there is even just a system of this on its own. It's a bit of like an
art where it's your job to interview them, speak to them, to draw insights out of them, to be the finger on the pulse for them. If they're busy with a
a job of leading a team, they sometimes might not be in tune with what's happening that day within their industry that they should be speaking about. But
somebody should be informing them of that. And to also like within a company, there's so much going on within a large organization, what are the things within
the brand that are happening that they should be speaking about. As one thing that happens is something happens within a company and everybody talks about the
exact same thing. And again looking at the data, I saw all unique moments where one thing would happen within the brand and everyone all
of a sudden turned up and became visible. Um, but not everyone needed to talk about that one thing and not everyone needed to use the exact same language in
how they spoke about it. Um, and I think that's uh another element of how we can help people and leaders within companies to be able to do this kind of thing. Um,
so yeah, just a bit of a closing statement like the people you need to hire, the culture you need to build within a company, the markets
you need to influence, the customer contracts you want to win. Like I said, the breadth of what this covers is so huge within a company and it's all
driven. I've seen it firsthand now of people being visible and the impact of that. And the reason that they're currently invisible is because nobody
within a company has made it a priority at all. Um, and the opportunity to get ahead of that curve exists now. I think this is
going to be a really trending thing that comes in over the next 5 years. So, yeah. Thank you.
